title: PostgreSQL Streaming Replication, Lag, and Dual-Primary Writes
objective: Run a primary and at least one streaming replica in Docker, measure a stale read caused by apply lag, promote the replica, and then reproduce a dual-primary write conflict unless the old primary is fenced from accepting clients.
whyThisMatters: A store you built yourself can hide how production databases actually ship bytes. The SWE curriculum never makes you promote a real replica or watch an old primary accept writes after failover. Until you have done both, 'we have a standby' is still folklore.
evidence: Compose (or equivalent) files and git history showing primary-only, then replica, then failover/fence steps as separate commits
A captured run that writes on the primary, delays apply on the replica, and reads a stale or missing row from the replica, with pg_stat_replication or equivalent numbers in the log
A second captured run of failover: promote, write on the new primary, then either a write on the old primary that diverges or a refused connection after fencing, with timeline / LSN values recorded
README stating the replica type (async or sync), the lag metric used, and the fencing method
Reflection notes answering the task questions
acceptanceCriteria: Primary and replica run as separate containers (or VMs) using PostgreSQL streaming replication, not a single-instance logical copy or a dump/restore loop.
The lag demonstration records a replica LSN or replay lag number at the moment of the stale read, and the same query on the primary returns the new row.
After promote, the new primary accepts a write that is not on the old primary's timeline; the captured log includes timeline IDs or LSNs for both sides.

README names either a working fence (old primary refuses clients or is shut down before clients are pointed at the new primary) or, if the dual-primary write was left unfenced on purpose, the conflicting row values on both nodes.
